What Makes a Good Unmasking Policy? A Controlled Study of Learned Unmasking in Diffusion Language Models

Jinya Sakurai    Xun Xu    Jaehong Yoon ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: NTU Singapore Affiliation: Institute for Advanced Intelligence and Computing (IAIC), A*STAR Affiliation: Centre for Frontier AI Research (CFAR), A*STAR
Abstract

Masked diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, but their efficiency depends on which predictions are committed. Learned unmasking policies improve the speed–accuracy trade-off, yet differ in supervision, inputs, and capacity, obscuring which choices matter. We view supervised policies as distilling a decoding procedure through a teacher and examine independently what the teacher labels as committable, on which states the policy imitates it, what the policy observes, and how much the number of function evaluations (NFE) must decrease to offset policy overhead. We find that labeling predictions matching the final output is overly permissive at low NFE, and hidden states are weak alone but can complement confidence. About a 10% NFE reduction suffices to offset policy overhead for policies up to 7.5M parameters across tested settings. We therefore train a policy on trajectory-contraction targets, which accept only commitments staying on a reference trajectory, using confidence and hidden states. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct, the resulting 856K-parameter policy achieves the best accuracy–NFE frontier and highest throughput on GSM8K, is competitive at moderate targets on MATH-500 and HumanEval, and largely transfers to Dream-7B-Instruct.

Code

1 Introduction

Building on discrete diffusion models (Hoogeboom et al., 2021; Austin et al., 2021a; Campbell et al., 2022; Lou et al., 2024), masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) (Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025; Sakurai et al., 2026) provide an alternative to the left-to-right generation of autoregressive models (Brown et al., 2020; Grattafiori et al., 2024; Qwen et al., 2025) by iteratively refining partially masked sequences and committing multiple tokens in parallel. Their efficiency, however, depends strongly on the unmasking policy, which decides which positions to commit at each step. Conservative policies require many denoising evaluations, whereas unmasking many tokens at once can produce mutually inconsistent tokens, as they are predicted independently given the same state. Such errors persist, since committed tokens are not revised later (Wu et al., 2026; Jazbec et al., 2026; Bao et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026). Recent work therefore adapts the number of committed tokens to the decoding state. Training-free methods do so using confidence (Wu et al., 2026) or entropy-based dependence control (Ben-Hamu et al., 2025), while learned policies are trained from data (Jazbec et al., 2026; Bao et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026).

Despite this progress, learned unmasking policies differ in several design choices at once: which positions are labeled as safe to commit, which decoding states are used for training, and what information the policy observes, often together with policy capacity. For example, whether backbone hidden states help cannot be judged, since the policies that use them also differ in size or supervision. Prior work reports the number of function evaluations (NFE) and throughput, but the NFE reduction needed to offset policy overhead across policy sizes, caching, and prompt lengths remains unclear.

We therefore revisit learned unmasking policies from a distillation perspective. Existing supervised policies (Bao et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026) can be viewed as distilling a fixed decoding procedure: the procedure is run on training prompts to obtain reference trajectories, a teacher derived from them labels which positions may be committed, and the policy imitates this teacher. This view separates what the teacher labels, on which states the policy imitates it, and what the policy observes; we vary one at a time, comparing choices from prior work with new candidates. First, existing teachers label a prediction as committable whenever it matches the final output. A correct token, however, is not necessarily safe to commit early, since its commitment changes the input to subsequent steps. We therefore introduce trajectory contraction, which labels a commitment as valid only when it directly reaches a later state of the reference trajectory, and compare it jointly with the choice of training states: reference trajectories or those induced by the labels. Second, as policy inputs, we compare confidence, probability margins, hidden representations, and confidence combined with hidden representations. Third, we measure both NFE and end-to-end throughput in tokens per second (TPS), and profile the policy overhead.

Our study shows that matching the final output is an overly permissive label in the low-NFE regime, with 28.7% of such positives leaving the reference trajectory when committed early, and that hidden representations are weak alone but can complement confidence. It also shows that, across the tested settings, a policy of up to 7.5M parameters pays off in throughput once it reduces NFE by more than about 10%. Based on these findings, we train a policy with trajectory-contraction targets on reference trajectories, taking confidence and hidden representations as input; it has only 856K parameters, about 0.01% of the backbone.

On LLaDA-8B-Instruct (Nie et al., 2025), our policy achieves the best accuracy–NFE frontier on GSM8K Cobbe et al. (2021), where it also attains the highest TPS at every accuracy target. On MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024) and HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), it reaches moderate accuracy targets with the fewest NFE and the highest TPS, whereas training-free methods are more efficient at the highest targets, and on MBPP Austin et al. (2021b) it performs comparably to the strongest baselines. Its advantage largely carries over to Dream-7B-Instruct (Ye et al., 2025) and, on mathematical reasoning, to unseen generation lengths.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    We show that matching the final output is an overly permissive commitment label in the low-NFE regime, and introduce trajectory contraction, which improves the accuracy–NFE frontier, with a further out-of-domain gain from supervision on reference trajectories.

  • •

    We show that backbone hidden states alone are a weak input, but can improve the frontier at high accuracy targets when combined with token confidence, and build on this an 856K-parameter policy.

  • •

    By profiling per-step latency, we show that policies of up to 7.5M parameters pay off in throughput once they reduce NFE by more than about 10% in the tested settings, and evaluate our policy across tasks, backbones, and generation lengths.

2 Related Work

Efficient unmasking. The efficiency and quality of dLLMs depend strongly on the order and degree of parallelism used for unmasking (Kim et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026). Training-free approaches exploit predictive uncertainty, decoding dynamics, or dependencies among candidate positions to determine which tokens can be committed in parallel (Ben-Hamu et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2026; Luxembourg et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026). Fast-dLLM is particularly relevant to our setting: it uses confidence-thresholded parallel decoding to reduce denoising steps while keeping the underlying dLLM frozen (Wu et al., 2026). Despite substantial progress, these methods prescribe the commitment rule at inference time rather than learning it from decoding experience.

Learning unmasking policies. Recent work instead learns where or when to commit tokens, using reinforcement learning, supervised oracle signals, ranking objectives, or learned dependency models (Hong et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Asano et al., 2026; Ringel et al., 2026). LUP learns a lightweight Transformer policy from confidence-based features using reinforcement learning (Jazbec et al., 2026). More directly related to our supervision setting, Learn2PD trains a lightweight filter from oracle token-correctness signals, whereas TraceLock derives commitment labels retrospectively from completed decoding traces and exploits richer hidden-state representations (Bao et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026). We study how to construct supervised commitment targets directly from Fast-dLLM trajectories and how to incorporate richer token-level information without sacrificing the efficiency of lightweight confidence-based policies.

3 Revisiting Unmasking Policy Learning

3.1 Problem Formulation

A masked dLLM generates a sequence x=(x1,…,xL)x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{L}) through partially masked states τ=(s0,…,sT)\tau=(s_{0},\ldots,s_{T}). At each step tt, the model produces token distributions pθ(⋅∣st)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}) for the masked positions ℳ⁡(st)\mathcal{M}(s_{t}), and an unmasking policy selects the positions to commit, At=πϕ​(zt)⊆ℳ⁡(st)A_{t}=\pi_{\phi}(z_{t})\subseteq\mathcal{M}(s_{t}), where ztz_{t} is the information available to the policy. The decoder then transitions to st+1=𝒞⁡(st,At)s_{t+1}=\mathcal{C}(s_{t},A_{t}), where 𝒞\mathcal{C} fills the selected positions with their greedy predictions, so the trajectory is deterministic given the policy decisions. Committing more positions per step reduces NFE, but premature commitments may degrade generation quality; a good policy achieves a favorable trade-off between the two.

3.2 Design Space and Protocol

We study supervised policies trained offline on a frozen backbone, such as Learn2PD (Bao et al., 2026) and TraceLock (Sun et al., 2026). These policies distill a fixed decoding procedure: the procedure is run on training prompts to obtain reference trajectories, from which each masked position at each state is labeled with a binary commitment target indicating whether it may be committed, and the policy is trained to predict these targets. Building such a policy requires deciding what counts as a correct commitment (the target), on which states the policy learns it (the training states; Section 3.3), and what the policy observes (the input; Section 3.4). Moreover, the policy is evaluated at every step, so its cost may offset the reduction in NFE (Section 3.5).

Existing methods vary simultaneously across multiple design axes, making it difficult to isolate the effect of individual design choices from their reported results. For example, LUP-hidden underperforms LUP-conf despite roughly 1000×1000\times more parameters (Jazbec et al., 2026) (Table 1). We therefore compare existing and newly introduced candidates for each design axis while holding the others fixed. We evaluate the commitment target and training states jointly in a 2×22\times 2 design to account for their interaction during teacher rollouts.

Setup. We use LLaDA-8B-Instruct (Nie et al., 2025) as the frozen backbone. Following Jazbec et al. (2026), all policies are trained on a mixture of the GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) and MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021) training sets, with reference trajectories generated by Fast-dLLM (Wu et al., 2026) at confidence threshold 0.90.9. Unless otherwise specified, we use generation length L=256L=256 and block length 3232, and evaluate zero-shot. We take the accuracy of one-by-one confidence-based decoding (Nie et al., 2025) as the reference and define target accuracy levels at 98%98\%, 95%95\%, and 90%90\% of it. For each method, we sweep its commitment threshold over a fixed grid (Section C.4) and compare the resulting accuracy–NFE trade-off against these targets. In this section, we evaluate on GSM8K (in-domain) and MBPP (out-of-domain) (Austin et al., 2021b), and all candidates share the same architecture, optimizer, and training schedule (Sections B.1 and C.3).

3.3 How Should Supervision Be Constructed?

Commitment targets. We consider two oracle criteria for defining supervision targets (Figure 1, panel (a)). Each oracle specifies which masked positions should be committed at a given state. The first, terminal agreement, is used by both Learn2PD (Bao et al., 2026) and TraceLock (Sun et al., 2026). It commits a position when its current prediction x^t,i\hat{x}_{t,i} matches the terminal token xi⋆x_{i}^{\star} of the reference trajectory: yt,itok=𝟙[x^t,i=xi⋆]y_{t,i}^{\mathrm{tok}}=\mathbbm{1}[\hat{x}_{t,i}=x_{i}^{\star}] (Section B.2). However, matching the terminal output does not guarantee that early commitment is safe: committing a token changes the input to subsequent evaluations and may alter predictions at other masked positions. We therefore introduce trajectory contraction (TC), which permits a commitment only if it directly reaches a state visited later in the reference trajectory. Let At→u=ℳ⁡(st)∖ℳ⁡(su)A_{t\rightarrow u}=\mathcal{M}(s_{t})\setminus\mathcal{M}(s_{u}) denote the positions committed between sts_{t} and a future state sus_{u} of the reference trajectory. We consider the commitment of this set valid if

𝒞⁡(st,At→u)=su.\mathcal{C}(s_{t},A_{t\rightarrow u})=s_{u}. (1)

This condition allows the intermediate states to be skipped while preserving the future reference state. We define ut⋆u_{t}^{\star} as the largest u>tu>t satisfying Equation 1, and set the target yt,itc=𝟙[i∈At→ut⋆]y_{t,i}^{\mathrm{tc}}=\mathbbm{1}[i\in A_{t\rightarrow u_{t}^{\star}}].

Training states. In addition to the commitment criterion, we consider two ways of constructing the states used for supervision (Figure 1, panel (b)). With reference trajectories, we collect training states from the fixed decoding procedure and apply the oracle at each state, including those the oracle would otherwise skip. With teacher-induced trajectories, we instead generate training states by repeatedly applying the oracle’s commitment decisions, so that supervision is provided only at the states it visits. TraceLock uses reference trajectories, whereas Learn2PD uses teacher-induced trajectories, referring to its oracle as the teacher.

Comparison. We compare the four combinations of two commitment targets (terminal agreement and trajectory contraction) and two training-state constructions (reference and teacher-induced trajectories), with the policy input fixed (Section B.1). As shown in Figure 2, replacing terminal agreement with trajectory contraction improves the frontier under both training-state constructions. On GSM8K, this change accounts for most of the gain, and both constructions perform comparably under contraction. On the out-of-domain MBPP, reference trajectories yield a further improvement, reaching the 98% target with 48.6 NFE versus 64.8 for teacher-induced trajectories. The gain from contraction is concentrated at low NFE; at the highest targets, terminal agreement can be more accurate (Section B.6).

Two observations help interpret these results. First, terminal agreement is more permissive: 28.7% of its positive labels fall outside the contraction set (Section B.2). These are correct predictions that follow a misprediction in the reference commitment order, so committing them early leads to a state the reference trajectory never visits. Second, teacher-induced trajectories retain only 34% (contraction) and 25% (terminal agreement) of the reference states (Section B.3). This reduced coverage may explain why reference trajectories transfer better to MBPP, although it has little effect on GSM8K.

3.4 What Information Should the Policy Use?

Input Candidates. Existing policies use token confidence (Learn2PD, LUP-conf) or backbone hidden representations (TraceLock, LUP-hidden). Beyond confidence, uncertainty statistics such as the top-two probability margin (Kim et al., 2025) and entropy (Xu et al., 2026) are also used to decide which tokens to unmask. For each masked position ii at step tt, we consider the token confidence ct,i=maxv⁡pθ​(xi=v∣st)c_{t,i}=\max_{v}p_{\theta}(x_{i}=v\mid s_{t}), the top-two probability margin Δt,i\Delta_{t,i} defined as the difference between the largest and second-largest token probabilities, and the backbone hidden representation ht,ih_{t,i}. We compare four input configurations:

zt,i∈{ct,i,ht,i,[ct,i,Δt,i],[ct,i,ht,i]}.z_{t,i}\in\left\{c_{t,i},\;h_{t,i},\;[c_{t,i},\Delta_{t,i}],\;[c_{t,i},h_{t,i}]\right\}. (2)

Each input is projected to a fixed hidden dimension and processed by the policy network fϕf_{\phi}, which predicts a commitment score for each masked position. To isolate the effect of the input from policy capacity (Section 3.2), we keep the policy architecture fixed across configurations, varying only the input projection.

Comparison. As shown in Figure 3, confidence provides a strong low-dimensional signal, whereas hidden states alone require substantially more NFEs to reach the same accuracy on both tasks. Adding the margin yields no consistent gain. Combining confidence with hidden states reaches the 98% and 95% targets with the fewest NFE on both tasks, e.g., 42.1 versus 52.9 NFE for confidence alone at the 98% target on GSM8K. At the 90% target, however, confidence alone is comparable on GSM8K and slightly more efficient on MBPP. On MATH-500 and HumanEval, the benefit is less consistent, and adding the margin is competitive or better at the highest targets (Section B.6). These results suggest that hidden states can complement confidence; we hypothesize that their high dimensionality makes it difficult for a lightweight policy to exploit them alone. This gain comes at a cost: projecting the 4096-dimensional hidden state increases the policy from 331K to 856K parameters.

3.5 Do NFE Gains Translate to Speedups?

The comparisons above measure decoding efficiency by NFE. While NFE captures the number of backbone evaluations, it does not account for the computational overhead of the policy itself. This trade-off depends on policy size (Table 1), including the 331K-to-856K increase from [c,h][c,h], and on backbone latency, which varies with prompt length and caching (Wu et al., 2026). We therefore profile per-step latency across these settings to determine how much NFE reduction is needed to improve throughput (Table 2; details in Section B.5). Besides our 331K and 856K policies, we include randomly initialized policies of 7.5M and 300M parameters, approximately matching TraceLock and LUP-hidden.

The key result is that the break-even NFE reduction remains small for lightweight policies. Up to 7.5M parameters, the policy adds a nearly constant cost of about 1.5 ms per step, at most 10% across all settings. Thus, reducing NFE by about 10% is sufficient to offset the policy overhead, regardless of prompt length or caching. Even a 300M policy, with up to 39% overhead, requires only about 28% fewer NFEs to break even. Although prefix caching reduces backbone latency by 73% at 2048 prompt tokens but only 5% at 128 tokens, the break-even threshold for policies up to 7.5M parameters remains around 10%. We evaluate the resulting throughput gains end to end in Sections 5.2 and 5.3.

4 Putting the Findings Together

We combine the findings into a single policy, which we call OnTrack: Finding 1 determines its supervision (Section 4.2), Finding 2 its input (Section 4.1), and Finding 3 keeps its overhead small.

4.1 Policy Architecture

Following Jazbec et al. (2026), we use a DiT-style policy network for unmasking decisions. For each masked position ii in the decoding step tt, the confidence ct,ic_{t,i} and hidden representation ht,ih_{t,i} are projected onto a shared dd-dimensional space and additively combined:

zt,i=Wc​ct,i+Wh​ht,i.z_{t,i}=W_{c}c_{t,i}+W_{h}h_{t,i}. (3)

Let zt=(zt,1,…,zt,L)z_{t}=(z_{t,1},\ldots,z_{t,L}) denote the resulting sequence. Conditioned on the mask state mtm_{t} and decoding step tt, the policy produces a sequence of commitment logits

ℓt=fϕ​(zt,mt,t),qt,i=σ⁡(ℓt,i).\ell_{t}=f_{\phi}(z_{t};m_{t},t),\qquad q_{t,i}=\sigma(\ell_{t,i}). (4)

Both projections and fϕf_{\phi} are trained jointly. With d=128d=128, the policy has 856K parameters, about 0.01% of the backbone (Architecture details are in Section A.1). At each step, the policy commits

At={i∈ℰt:qt,i>γ},A_{t}=\left\{i\in\mathcal{E}_{t}:q_{t,i}>\gamma\right\}, (5)

where ℰt\mathcal{E}_{t} is the set of masked positions in the current block and γ\gamma is an inference-time commitment threshold (Section A.3).

4.2 Policy Training

We generate reference trajectories as described in Section 3.2 and retain those whose final answer is correct. For each reference state sts_{t}, the target is the trajectory-contraction label yt,i=yt,itcy_{t,i}=y^{\mathrm{tc}}_{t,i} (Section 3.3), which marks the positions in the furthest valid contraction At→ut⋆A_{t\rightarrow u_{t}^{\star}}. We optimize binary cross-entropy over eligible positions,

ℒ=−∑t,i∈ℰt[yt,ilogqt,i+(1−yt,i)log(1−qt,i)].\displaystyle\mathcal{L}=-\!\sum_{t,\ i\in\mathcal{E}_{t}}\left[y_{t,i}\log q_{t,i}+(1-y_{t,i})\log(1-q_{t,i})\right].

The complete target-construction procedure is provided in Section A.2.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks and backbones. We follow the setup of Section 3.2 and extend the evaluation to MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024) and HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), so that GSM8K and MATH-500 evaluate in-domain generalization and HumanEval and MBPP evaluate out-of-domain generalization to code. We additionally evaluate on Dream-7B-Instruct (Ye et al., 2025) (Section 5.4); implementation details are provided in Appendix C.

Baselines. We compare against two training-free methods, Fast-dLLM (Wu et al., 2026), which commits positions whose confidence exceeds a threshold, and EB-Sampler (Ben-Hamu et al., 2025), which commits positions within an entropy budget, and against Learn2PD (Bao et al., 2026), a learned policy for which we use the official checkpoint. We do not include LUP (Jazbec et al., 2026) or TraceLock (Sun et al., 2026), as no trained checkpoints are publicly available for either method.

Evaluation protocol. We report accuracy on GSM8K and MATH-500 and Pass@1 on HumanEval and MBPP, together with NFE and TPS, with all throughput measured on the same hardware and configuration (Section C.5).

5.2 Main Results on LLaDA

In-domain reasoning. On GSM8K, our policy yields the best frontier and reaches 98% of the reference accuracy with the fewest NFE (Figure 4, top). On MATH-500, it reaches the 95% target with the fewest NFE, but its accuracy saturates just below the 98% target, whereas EB-Sampler and Fast-dLLM exceed the reference at larger NFE.

Out-of-domain code generation. Although the policy is trained only on mathematical reasoning, it transfers to code. On HumanEval, it reaches 90% of the reference accuracy with the fewest NFE, but Fast-dLLM is more efficient at the 95% target, and only Fast-dLLM and EB-Sampler reach the 98% target. On MBPP, our policy reaches the 95% and 98% targets with the fewest NFE, whereas Learn2PD and Fast-dLLM are more efficient at the 90% target. Paired-bootstrap confidence intervals (Table 27) show that the NFE gains on GSM8K exceed evaluation noise against all baselines except EB-Sampler at the 98% target.

Throughput. The NFE reductions carry over to throughput (Figure 4, bottom): at matched accuracy, our policy achieves the highest TPS on GSM8K across targets and on MATH-500 and HumanEval at moderate targets. On MBPP, it is close to the fastest baseline at the 95% and 98% targets but slower at the 90% target. Consistent with Finding 3, the 856K-parameter policy’s NFE advantage outweighs the overhead of evaluating it per step.

5.3 Compatibility with Prefix Caching

We evaluate our policy and baselines with prefix caching (Wu et al., 2026) on GSM8K using zero-shot and four-shot prompts, following the latency analysis in Section 3.5. To ensure consistent accuracy targets across cached and uncached decoding, we use the uncached one-by-one baseline under the same prompting as the reference (78.0% zero-shot and 79.9% four-shot).

Fewer NFE still means faster decoding. The reduction in NFE carries over to caching (Table 3): with four-shot prompts, our policy remains the fastest at 98% of the reference accuracy. Despite the reduced backbone latency and increased relative policy overhead, its NFE advantage translates into higher throughput.

Accuracy sensitivity. Caching reduces our policy’s accuracy by up to about two percentage points, while the baselines are less affected (Figure 10). With zero-shot prompts, Fast-dLLM overtakes our policy at the 98% accuracy target, although ours remains the fastest at 95% (Table 3; see Section 7).

5.4 Generalization Across Backbones

We next examine whether our design transfers to a different dLLM. We apply the same procedure to Dream-7B-Instruct, training a separate policy with the same training data, trajectory-contraction supervision, and policy-training procedure. Since Dream has a hidden dimension of 3584, the policy has 790K parameters.

Figure 5 shows that the advantage of our policy is largely preserved. It yields the best frontier on HumanEval, where it exceeds the reference accuracy with the fewest NFE, and reaches 98% of the reference accuracy on MATH-500 with the fewest NFE. On GSM8K, it reaches 95% of the reference accuracy with the fewest NFE but saturates slightly below the reference, where Fast-dLLM and EB-Sampler are more accurate at larger NFE. On MBPP, all methods reach the targets within a narrow NFE range and perform comparably.

5.5 Generalization Across Sequence Lengths

We finally examine whether the learned policy generalizes across generation lengths without retraining. Following the length-transfer setting of Jazbec et al. (2026), we train the policy with L=256L=256 and evaluate the same checkpoint at L=128L=128 and L=512L=512 on GSM8K and MATH-500, keeping the block length fixed at 3232.

As shown in Figure 6, the policy largely retains its advantage under both length shifts: it yields the best or comparable frontier up to 95% of the reference accuracy at both lengths, and at L=128L=128 it reaches 98% on MATH-500 with the fewest NFE. At L=512L=512, it saturates below 98% on MATH-500, where Fast-dLLM and EB-Sampler exceed the reference at larger NFE. When the length shift is combined with the domain shift to code, however, the policy falls behind Fast-dLLM and EB-Sampler on HumanEval and MBPP (Section C.6), indicating that it tolerates either shift alone but not both.

6 Conclusion

We revisited learned unmasking policies for dLLMs through a controlled study of supervision, inputs, and overhead. Trajectory-contraction targets improve the accuracy–NFE frontier mainly at low NFE, with a further out-of-domain gain from reference trajectories. Hidden representations are weak alone but can complement confidence at high accuracy targets. Policies of up to 7.5M parameters pay off in throughput once they reduce NFE by more than about 10% in the tested settings. Building on these findings, our 856K-parameter policy reaches moderate accuracy targets with the best or comparable efficiency across two backbones, transfers from mathematical reasoning to code, and converts its NFE reductions into throughput gains.

7 Limitations

Training and evaluation scope. Our policy is trained only on mathematical reasoning data at a single generation length (L=256L=256) with a fixed block length. It transfers to code at the training length and to other lengths on mathematical tasks, but its advantage does not persist when both shifts occur together (Section 5.5). Training on multiple domains and generation lengths is a natural remedy that we leave to future work.

High-accuracy regime. On some tasks (MATH-500 on LLaDA and GSM8K on Dream), the accuracy of our policy saturates slightly below the reference, even with conservative thresholds, whereas training-free methods reach the reference at larger NFE. Our policy is therefore most beneficial at moderate accuracy targets, and closing this gap may require supervision that covers more conservative commitment behavior.

Sensitivity to backbone features. Approximate inference such as prefix caching reduces the accuracy of our policy by up to about two points, whereas confidence-based baselines are essentially unaffected (Section 5.3). The drop persists even when the policy unmasks one token per step, so it concerns which tokens are committed rather than how many. A plausible cause is that the policy consumes backbone hidden representations, which caching perturbs; making learned unmasking policies robust to approximate inference is left to future work.

8 Ethical Considerations

Environmental impact. This work aims to reduce the computational cost of inference with diffusion language models, potentially lowering energy consumption. However, the overall environmental impact depends on deployment scale, as improved efficiency may encourage greater model usage.

Potential risks. Faster inference may facilitate large-scale generation of misleading or harmful content. Our method does not modify backbone parameters and only determines when to commit the backbone’s predictions. It therefore inherits the capabilities, biases, and failure modes of the underlying models. Changes in decoding may also affect output safety, which we do not explicitly evaluate.

Artifacts and licensing. All datasets (GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024), HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021b)) and models (LLaDA-8B-Instruct (Nie et al., 2025) and Dream-7B-Instruct (Ye et al., 2025)) are publicly available and used in accordance with their licenses. Our implementation builds on the publicly released codebase of Learning Unmasking Policies for Diffusion Language Models (Jazbec et al., 2026), with modifications for our proposed policy training and decoding methods. We collect no new data involving human subjects.

Use of AI assistants. We used AI assistants to support code development, figure preparation, and language polishing of the manuscript. All AI-assisted outputs were reviewed and verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the code, figures, and scientific content.

What Makes a Good Unmasking Policy? A Controlled Study of Learned Unmasking in Diffusion Language Models

Supplementary Material

Appendix A Method Details

A.1 Policy Architecture

Our policy follows the DiT-style architecture of Jazbec et al. (2026). We use the token confidence ct,ic_{t,i} and hidden representation ht,ih_{t,i} defined in Section 3.4. The two signals are independently projected to a shared dd-dimensional representation:

zt,iconf\displaystyle z^{\mathrm{conf}}_{t,i} =Wc​ct,i+bc,\displaystyle=W_{c}c_{t,i}+b_{c}, (6)
zt,ihid\displaystyle z^{\mathrm{hid}}_{t,i} =Wh​ht,i+bh,\displaystyle=W_{h}h_{t,i}+b_{h}, (7)

where Wc∈ℝd×1W_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times 1} and Wh∈ℝd×dhW_{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{h}}. The hidden-state stream is added to the confidence representation:

zt,i=zt,iconf+zt,ihid.z_{t,i}=z^{\mathrm{conf}}_{t,i}+z^{\mathrm{hid}}_{t,i}. (8)

Let zt=(zt,1,…,zt,L)z_{t}=(z_{t,1},\ldots,z_{t,L}) denote the resulting sequence and mt=(mt,1,…,mt,L)m_{t}=(m_{t,1},\ldots,m_{t,L}) the corresponding mask state. The policy produces commitment logits

ℓt=fϕ​(zt,mt,t),qt,i=σ⁡(ℓt,i).\ell_{t}=f_{\phi}(z_{t};m_{t},t),\qquad q_{t,i}=\sigma(\ell_{t,i}). (9)

Following Jazbec et al. (2026), we use a single DiT-style transformer block. Token positions are encoded through RoPE (Su et al., 2024) in self-attention.

The confidence projection, hidden-state projection, and policy network fϕf_{\phi} are optimized jointly, while the dLLM backbone remains frozen throughout training. The policy produces logits for all sequence positions, while commitment is restricted to masked positions in the current block, as described in Section A.3.

A.2 Trajectory-Contraction Teacher

We construct training targets from a reference trajectory

τref=(s0,…,sT).\tau^{\mathrm{ref}}=(s_{0},\ldots,s_{T}). (10)

For each state sts_{t} and future state sus_{u}, u>tu>t, we define

At→u=ℳ⁡(st)∖ℳ⁡(su),A_{t\rightarrow u}=\mathcal{M}(s_{t})\setminus\mathcal{M}(s_{u}), (11)

as the set of positions committed between the two states. Following Section 3.3, the segment from sts_{t} to sus_{u} can be contracted into a single decoding step when

𝒞⁡(st,At→u)=su.\mathcal{C}(s_{t},A_{t\rightarrow u})=s_{u}. (12)

For each reference state, we select the furthest future state satisfying this criterion,

ut⋆=max⁡{u>t:𝒞⁡(st,At→u)=su},u_{t}^{\star}=\max\left\{u>t:\mathcal{C}(s_{t},A_{t\rightarrow u})=s_{u}\right\}, (13)

and use the corresponding commitment set

At⋆=At→ut⋆A_{t}^{\star}=A_{t\rightarrow u_{t}^{\star}} (14)

to define the binary teacher targets

yt,i=[i∈At⋆].y_{t,i}=\mathbbm{1}\!\left[i\in A_{t}^{\star}\right]. (15)

Validity is monotone in uu: since At→u′⊆At→uA_{t\rightarrow u^{\prime}}\subseteq A_{t\rightarrow u} for u′<uu^{\prime}<u, if Equation 12 holds for uu, it also holds for every t<u′<ut<u^{\prime}<u. Targets therefore require no backbone evaluations beyond those of the reference trajectory.

We construct these targets independently for every st∈τrefs_{t}\in\tau^{\mathrm{ref}} and retain all states of the reference trajectory for policy training. Algorithm 1 summarizes the procedure.

A.3 Decoding

Block diffusion partitions the generated sequence into fixed blocks B1,…,BKB_{1},\ldots,B_{K} and allows tokens to be committed only within the current block BkB_{k}. At each decoding step, the eligible positions are ℰt=ℳ⁡(st)∩Bk\mathcal{E}_{t}=\mathcal{M}(s_{t})\cap B_{k}, and the policy commits

At={i∈ℰt:qt,i>γ},A_{t}=\left\{i\in\mathcal{E}_{t}:q_{t,i}>\gamma\right\}, (16)

where γ\gamma is the commitment threshold. If no eligible position exceeds γ\gamma, we commit the eligible position with the highest policy score. The selected positions are filled with the corresponding top-1 predictions of the frozen backbone.

Appendix B Controlled Study Details

B.1 Experimental Setup

Controlled experiments follow the training and decoding configuration in Sections C.2 and C.3 and are evaluated on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024), HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021b). The reference accuracy is that of one-by-one confidence-based decoding (78.0% on GSM8K, 38.8% on MATH-500, 45.1% on HumanEval, and 52.9% on MBPP), and the accuracy targets are 98%, 95%, and 90% of it. For each policy, we sweep the commitment threshold γ\gamma over the grid in Table 12 and report the frontier of non-dominated operating points. Each comparison varies a single factor while keeping the others fixed, as summarized in Table 5.

B.2 Commitment Target Construction

Trajectory-contraction targets are constructed as described in Section A.2.

Terminal agreement. We use the final token of the reference trajectory, generated by Fast-dLLM with threshold 0.90.9, as the terminal target xi⋆x_{i}^{\star}. This corresponds to the labeling rule shared by Learn2PD (Bao et al., 2026) and TraceLock (Sun et al., 2026), which label a prediction by its agreement with the terminal output of a fixed decoding procedure. For teacher-induced trajectories, the same xi⋆x_{i}^{\star} is used even after the trajectory departs from the reference.

Agreement–contraction mismatch. Since a valid contraction commits only tokens that match the reference trajectory, contraction positives are always a subset of terminal-agreement positives. Over all reference trajectories, 28.7% of terminal-agreement positives violate trajectory contraction, i.e., they are correct tokens whose commitment at sts_{t} would leave the reference trajectory, and 56.0% of reference states contain at least one such violation. The fraction is consistent across datasets (28.5% on GSM8K and 29.1% on MATH).

B.3 Training-Trajectory Construction

Reference trajectories. Targets are computed on every state of the reference trajectory, and the policy is trained on all of these states.

Teacher-induced trajectories. Starting from s0s_{0}, we repeatedly apply the teacher, committing every positively labeled position, and train on the resulting states. Under trajectory contraction, the teacher jumps from sts_{t} to sut⋆s_{u_{t}^{\star}}, so the induced trajectory is a subsequence of the reference trajectory and its targets are inherited from it. Under terminal agreement, the induced states generally leave the reference trajectory; we therefore run the backbone on each induced state to obtain new predictions and recompute targets. Table 6 reports the number of training states under each configuration. Teacher-induced trajectories retain only a fraction of the reference states: 34.0% under trajectory contraction and 25.4% under terminal agreement.

B.4 Policy-Input Study

Inputs. The confidence ct,ic_{t,i} and margin Δt,i\Delta_{t,i} are computed from the backbone’s predictive distribution at each masked position. The hidden representation ht,i∈ℝ4096h_{t,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{4096} is taken from the final layer of the backbone. Each input is linearly projected to d=128d=128 dimensions before entering the shared policy network fϕf_{\phi}.

Parameter counts. Table 7 lists the parameter count of each policy. All policies share the same network fϕf_{\phi}; the differences arise only from the input projections.

B.5 Per-Step Latency Profiling

Table 8 reports the absolute per-step latencies underlying Table 2. They are obtained by profiling LLaDA-8B-Instruct on a single H200 GPU with batch size 1, generation length L=256L=256, block length 32, and commitment threshold 0.90.9, using synthetic prompts of 128 to 2048 tokens. Each entry is the median over three decoding runs of the steady-state per-step latency, which comprises the backbone forward pass, the policy forward pass, and per-step bookkeeping. Without caching, the backbone forward pass processes the full sequence; with prefix caching, it reuses cached states, and the full forward pass that opens each block is excluded. Within each row, the backbone latency is the median over all policy configurations, so differences across columns reflect only the policy and bookkeeping.

Policy sizes.

The 331K and 856K columns are the trained Conf. and Conf.+Hidden policies used in our experiments. To see how the overhead grows with policy size, we add two larger policies whose parameter counts roughly match those of policies in prior work: the 7.5M policy is about the size of the TraceLock (Sun et al., 2026) network, and the 300M policy is about the size of the LUP-hidden (Jazbec et al., 2026) network. These two policies do not reproduce the architectures of those methods. Both are scaled-up versions of our Conf.+Hidden policy, with widths chosen to approximately match the target parameter counts. The 7.5M policy uses hidden width 512, feed-forward width 2400, and 8 attention heads, with one block in each of the confidence and hidden streams (7.52M parameters). The 300M policy uses hidden width 2048, feed-forward width 7296, and 16 heads, with four blocks in each stream (300.3M parameters). Both policies are randomly initialized and are used only for latency measurement. This does not bias the measurement, because the cost of a policy forward pass depends on its architecture and input shape, not on its weights, and the per-step latency is measured independently of the decisions the policy makes.

B.6 Results on MATH-500 and HumanEval

Figures 8 and 9 repeat the comparisons of Sections 3.3 and 3.4 on MATH-500 and HumanEval, with the same configurations (Table 5).

Supervision. On HumanEval, combining trajectory contraction with reference trajectories yields the best frontier throughout, reaches the 90% target with the fewest NFE, and is the only configuration to reach the 95% target, whereas terminal agreement on reference trajectories remains below 90% at all operating points. On MATH-500, the same combination yields the best frontier up to the 95% target but saturates just below 98%, whereas the other configurations reach 98% at larger NFE, with terminal agreement on reference trajectories exceeding the reference accuracy. Trajectory contraction thus mainly improves the low-NFE regime, consistent with Finding 1.

Policy input. Hidden states alone remain below 95% of the reference accuracy on MATH-500 and below 90% on HumanEval. On MATH-500, combining confidence with hidden states yields the best frontier up to the 95% target but saturates just below 98%, whereas adding the margin reaches 98% with the fewest NFE and the highest accuracy, exceeding the reference. On HumanEval, all confidence-based inputs perform comparably up to the 90% target, but only the margin and hidden-state combinations reach 95%, and none reaches 98%.

Appendix C Experimental Details

C.1 Datasets and Prompt Templates

Datasets. We train on the GSM8K training split (openai/gsm8k) and the MATH training split (ankner/math-500). For MATH, we exclude 15 examples whose gold answers cannot be parsed by the answer verifier, leaving 7,485 examples. The resulting 14,958 training examples are concatenated and shuffled with seed 42. During training, prompts exceeding 256 tokens are left-truncated to retain the last 256 tokens. Evaluation prompts are not truncated, and no evaluation examples are used for training.

Table 9 summarizes the dataset sizes. All evaluations use zero-shot prompting unless otherwise stated. GSM8K uses the openai/gsm8k test split, MATH-500 uses HuggingFaceH4/MATH-500, HumanEval uses openai/openai_humaneval, and MBPP uses the sanitized test split of google-research-datasets/mbpp.

Prompt templates. We use task-specific instruction prompts with the backbone’s chat template. For GSM8K and MATH, we use the same prompt for training and evaluation, instructing the model to solve problems step by step and provide the final answer in \boxed{}. For HumanEval and MBPP, we follow the prompts from lm-eval. HumanEval provides a function signature and docstring, while MBPP provides a task description and test cases. For both tasks, generation continues from a partially provided code block.

Answer verification. For GSM8K and MATH, we extract and verify the final boxed answer using math-verify v0.8.0. The same procedure is used to select correct reference trajectories for training.

C.2 Policy Optimization

We train the full policy jointly with AdamW. Training takes approximately 3 hours and 15 minutes on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. Unless otherwise specified, all policy-training experiments use the hyperparameters in Table 10.

C.3 Training and Decoding Configuration

Following Jazbec et al. (2026), we train the policy on the training splits of GSM8K and MATH. We retain only reference trajectories whose final answer is correct, yielding 9,169 trajectories. No code-generation examples are used for policy training; HumanEval and MBPP therefore evaluate out-of-domain generalization from mathematical reasoning to code.

Reference trajectories are generated by Fast-dLLM (Wu et al., 2026) with a confidence threshold of 0.90.9. We use generation length L=256L=256 and block length 3232 for both trajectory collection and the main evaluation. For the length-transfer evaluation at L=512L=512 (Section 5.5), we additionally apply End-of-Text Prediction (EoTP) (Bao et al., 2026) to all methods: once an end-of-text token has been committed, all remaining masked positions after it are filled with end-of-text tokens, and decoding terminates. As a result, the NFE at L=512L=512 can be smaller than LL even for one-by-one decoding. The trajectory-generation temperature is set to zero.

The frozen LLaDA-8B-Instruct backbone is loaded in bfloat16, while policy computation is performed in float32. The backbone parameters remain frozen throughout policy training.

C.4 Parameter Grids

Table 12 summarizes the commitment rule of each method and the parameter swept to obtain operating points. OnTrack (Ours), Learn2PD, and Fast-dLLM commit every eligible position whose score exceeds a threshold γ\gamma, which we sweep over the same grid γ∈{0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8,0.85,0.9,0.94,0.96,0.98,0.99}\gamma\in\{0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8,0.85,0.9,0.94,0.96,0.98,0.99\} for all three methods. EB-Sampler (Ben-Hamu et al., 2025) sorts positions by confidence and commits the longest prefix whose total entropy minus its maximum entropy does not exceed a budget ϵ\epsilon, which we sweep over ϵ∈{0,0.001,0.003,0.01,0.03,0.1,0.3,1,3,10}\epsilon\in\{0,0.001,0.003,0.01,0.03,0.1,0.3,1,3,10\}.

C.5 Throughput Measurement

All throughput measurements are performed on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU (141 GB) with batch size 1, using LLaDA-8B-Instruct in bfloat16 with FlashAttention-2 (Dao, 2024). TPS is computed as the number of generated tokens, excluding tokenizer special tokens, divided by the sampler wall-clock time, which includes both backbone and policy evaluations but excludes tokenization, detokenization, and answer scoring. For each prompt, we call torch.cuda.synchronize immediately before and after the sampler call and time the interval with a high-resolution host timer. No warm-up runs are performed; each prompt is decoded once (a single pass over the full evaluation set), with only one generation process per GPU. Timing is aggregated per dataset and decoding configuration as the total number of generated tokens over the total sampler time, i.e., a token-weighted average rather than a mean of per-prompt rates.

C.6 Additional Results

For the prefix caching experiments (Section 5.3), Figure 10 shows the accuracy–throughput frontiers on GSM8K under zero-shot and four-shot prompting. Our policy exhibits greater accuracy sensitivity to caching than the baselines, while four-shot prompting yields substantial throughput improvements with caching.

For generalization across sequence lengths (Section 5.5), Figure 11 shows the frontiers on HumanEval and MBPP at L=128L=128 and L=512L=512, complementing Figure 6. The corresponding operating points, together with those for all other figures, are listed in Appendix D.
